summary: Esopus Meadows Light on the Hudson flats near Esopus: a stone house first lit in 1839, the wooden house of 1871-72 put out in 1965, and relit in 2003 after restoration.

lens.where: original fifth-order lens; current optic removed (USLHS record); relit 2003 (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Second light, completed 1871 and first lit 26 Aug 1872; 53 ft (Hudson River Lighthouses). The record gives 17.0 m and the USLHS table 37 ft; not used.
Rectangular two-story dwelling with the tower at one end (LighthouseFriends); Hudson River Lighthouses describes it as square.

access.note: Reached by water; special tours by arrangement; boaters may stop when the open flag is flying (Hudson River Lighthouses).

facts.agency: Save Esopus Lighthouse Commission (owner since 2002, per LighthouseFriends and Hudson River Lighthouses); U.S. Coast Guard before 2002

events.note: Congress appropriates $3,000 for a lighthouse at Esopus Meadows, not begun because the cost doubled
Second $3,000 appropriation, 3 March 1837; further $3,000 on 7 July 1838
Stone dwelling 34 by 20 ft with octagonal tower on a wooden pier 41 by 50 ft
Four lamps and reflectors; first keeper Jeremiah Teerpenning
Sixth-order lens replaces the lamps and reflectors
Dwelling unfit for winter occupancy; pier dilapidated (LighthouseFriends; Hudson River Lighthouses)
Congress authorizes $25,000 on 15 July 1870 to rebuild; work starts the next spring
Second light: wood frame, clapboard, 100 ft southeast of the first, on 250 piles and a granite pier; design by Albert R. Dow
Second light first shows from a fifth-order Fresnel lens on 26 August 1872 (LighthouseFriends)
Fog bell operated by machinery, in service from the opening of navigation (Light-House Board)
Keeper George R. Humphrey resigns the day after an inspector finds him absent (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper Thomas J. Murray rescues two men and a woman whose ice boat broke through the ice (14 January; Lighthouse Service Bulletin 1915)
Keeper Emanuel Weber falls into the river recovering the station boat (14 March); dies 20 April 1936; Sylvia Weber acting keeper (LighthouseFriends; roster)
Light automated and put out on 18 August 1965; keeper line ends with Alfred J. Vaughan (LighthouseFriends; roster)
Title passes to the Save Esopus Lighthouse Commission on 22 September 2002 under the pilot disposal programme (LighthouseFriends)
Coast Guard returns the light to the lantern room on 31 May 2003 (LighthouseFriends)
Floating dock installed in May; lighthouse opened to visitors arriving by boat in July (LighthouseFriends)

LighthouseFriends gives 26 August 1872 for the first showing of the fifth-order lens in the second light; the 1871 date is the year the house was completed.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's single wooden tower built 1839 merges two lights: the stone house of 1839 (LighthouseFriends) and the wooden tower completed in 1871 (Hudson River Lighthouses; first lit 1872). The story describes both.

LighthouseFriends and the record give 1839 for the first light. The Hudson River Lighthouses page gives the first light's span as 1837-1871, with Congress's appropriations of 1837 and 1838 to complete it. The story gives 1839 for the stone house, following LighthouseFriends, and mentions the appropriations.

notes_for_editor: Sources read: LighthouseFriends (cite 1; secondary; the 1831-1872 construction history, the 1903 and 1934 inspections, the 1936 incident, the 1965 automation, the 2002 title, the 2003 relight, and the 2010 visits); U.S. Lighthouse Society place record and roster, 36 lines (cite 2); Light-House Board annual report 1891-1892, scan p. 79 (cite 3); Lighthouse Service Bulletin No. 37 (January 1915), printed p. 151, PDF p. 7 (cite 4); Hudson River Lighthouses page (cite 5; owner, visiting, appropriations, construction details). The 1915 rescue entry prints 'January 14' with no year; the year used is the Bulletin volume's, and the USLHS index also gives page 151. Not checked: NRHP 79001638 (the nomination is not digitised; the PDF is the 76-character placeholder); Light-House Board volumes before 1891 (not in the corpus), so the 1831-1870 appropriations rest on LighthouseFriends and the Hudson River Lighthouses page; New York newspapers in Chronicling America (one earlier search returned unrelated pages); the 1936 papers. Disagreements left in the story: the dwelling's shape (LighthouseFriends rectangular; Hudson River Lighthouses square); the east side's droop (LighthouseFriends sixteen inches; Hudson River Lighthouses eighteen); the commission's history (LighthouseFriends dates the relaunch to 1997; Hudson River Lighthouses says it leased the light in 1990 to begin restoration and reorganised in 1997); the keeper Manny Resendes (Hudson River Lighthouses: last civilian keeper before the Coast Guard took over in 1939; the roster lists him to 1944; LighthouseFriends gives 1937 to 1944). The Hudson River Lighthouses page also names a newly chartered 'Esopus Meadows Lighthouse' as the holder of stewardship in 2002; the USLHS record and that page's own owner field name the Save Esopus Lighthouse Commission, so the commission is used. Keepers: Anna Warren ('de facto', Hudson River Lighthouses, 1886-1891) against Omar Warren (roster 1885-1891; Hudson River Lighthouses 1885-1886). The Hudson River Lighthouses page pairs some keepers with a wife in brackets ('Jonathan (& Sara) Cole', 'Andrew A. (& Rebecca) McLintock', 'Emanuel (& Sylvia) Weber', 'Manuel (& Ellie) Resendes'); those entries do not say whether the wife kept the light in her own right, so they are not added as lines. John J. Bretz (Hudson River Lighthouses, 1944) is not on the roster and is recorded with that note. John J. Dixon (Hudson River Lighthouses) is John T. Dixon on the roster. The roster gives Sylvia Weber as principal keeper; LighthouseFriends calls her a temporary keeper; the role is recorded as acting keeper with the archive dates. Post-1960 names: the Coast Guard lines and John F. Monahan, David F. Bennett and others are kept to the roster; the Hudson River Lighthouses page's 1961 anecdote about a keeper is left out as a personal detail about a man whose connection ended after about 1960. The keeper roster's person slugs match roster.py output. Length and shape: about 1,120 words in six chapters. The evidence is moderate: the 1891 report and the 1915 Bulletin each give one entry, and the rest is the roster and two secondary pages. Each of the six chapters carries a sourced paragraph, so the story keeps all six rather than cutting to the moderate table's 2-4 chapters; the editor can merge chapters if preferred.
